title: Relative clauses
examples: When do I use commas with relative clauses?
What is the difference between who and which?
Can I use 'that' in every situation?

explain.say: Today we learn to join sentences with relative clauses. These clauses give extra information about a noun.
We use who for people and which for things. Remember to choose the right word for the noun.

draw.text: Who for people, Which for things

explain.say: Sometimes you can use that instead of who or which. This is often the shortest way to connect ideas.
Now we look at commas. Commas change the meaning of the information we add.
Defining clauses are essential; they tell us which specific person or thing we mean. No commas are used here.
Non-defining clauses give extra, non-essential details. These always need commas to set them apart.

faq.a: Use who when the relative clause is about a person. Use which when the clause is about a thing or animal.
asks: Do I use who or which for people?
What word do I use for objects?

faq.q: Are commas always needed when I add extra information?
faq.a: No, commas are only needed if the information is extra and not necessary to identify the noun. If it is necessary, use no commas.
asks: Do I always need commas for extra facts?

faq.q: Can I use 'that' in every situation?
faq.a: You can use that in many cases, but you should not use it when the clause is non-defining. Non-defining clauses need commas.

faq.q: What is the difference between defining and non-defining?
faq.a: Defining information is needed to know which noun you mean. Non-defining information is just extra detail about something already known.
asks: What is the difference between the two types?

faq.q: If I remove the clause, does the sentence still make sense?
faq.a: If the sentence still makes perfect sense without the clause, it is likely non-defining and needs commas. If it does not make sense, it is defining and needs no commas.
asks: How do I check if commas are right?
Can I test the sentence without the clause?

facts: Use who for people and which for things.
Defining clauses are essential and use no commas.
Non-defining clauses provide extra detail and use commas.
The relative pronoun can be who, which, or that.

quiz.say: The scientist who discovered penicillin was Alexander Fleming.
quiz.show: The scientist who discovered penicillin was Alexander Fleming.
quiz.why: We use who because 'scientist' is a person, and the clause is essential to identify him.

wrong.1: Which is used for things, not people.
wrong.2: While 'that' can sometimes replace 'who', using 'who' is clearer for people.
wrong.3: No comma is needed because the information is defining and necessary.

quiz.say: My best friend, who lives nearby, is coming over later.
quiz.show: My best friend, who lives nearby, is coming over later.
quiz.why: We use commas because the information about where she lives is extra detail, not needed to identify her.

wrong.1: No commas suggest the information is essential, which is not the case here.
wrong.2: Adding a period changes the sentence structure incorrectly.
